items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: He was called king, Johnny Dunn, played with Mamie Smith.

ctx.x: Seeing as how Armstrong, can you hold it over here soon? Did I just want to give it a hand? Seeing as how, you know, Armstrong went up to Chicago and made a big name for himself, in a way, he sort of put himself above that, all that competitiveness and savage competition when he became famous. And I'm just wondering if, do you think he ever took his fame for granted or was he always trying to expand it?

No, he was a happy man. He, he was so acclaimed by everybody. Every trumpet player, everybody who, who, who played a horn, paid him homage somewhere or other, or they stayed a distance from him. Whole lot of great white trumpet players, legitimate trumpet players, never went near Louis. You dig, they may have looked, but they dismissed him as, not exactly black, but that kind of style, that ain't, well, that's something to do with it too, but you always, you don't always put it on being black. He could have been…
Was Johnny Dunn from New Orleans?

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And I say, “I thought it was Bessie Smith or the ones that recorded.” Bessie Smith or Clara Smith, or the other one, Mamie Smith.

ctx.x: In Harlem. It’s a club on 133rd Street. Later it became Dickie Wells’s nightclub. It was on a basement on the ground floor with a club called the . . . a funny name. The Fun Box? No. The Fun Box is near . . . The Mad House, on the first floor. The Mad

House. Downstairs was the Nest Club. I played in there. You go to work at ten o’clock at night and you come out ten o’clock in the morning, because it was a depression that set in, and we didn’t get a crowd until after three o’clock in the morning. Three, four, five . . . five o’clock, the band go on, because you sit there all night. There might be parties drifting in. It was just to winter. I had never seen snow, real snow falling. The doorman there, he had seven singers there: Mamie Smith, Clara Smith, and…

give him a chance. You can make believe he’s playing when he ain’t, and in two weeks he be knowing enough how to play the guitar. Give him the basics.” Harry says, “It’s all right with me. It’s all right with me,” he said, “but I ain’t got no money to buy him no guitar.” Harry said, “We’ll try to get him a guitar. We just opened this place. You see, we’re trying to pay the overhead and pay the cook and pay them girls and all that.” Say, “I’m about to close up.” He said, “No, don’t close up. Just let me have him…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Mamie, the last I seen her, she was a tired old lady around New York.

ctx.x: Columbia. He went to Victor first. Victor laughed at him. He made a fool(?) of Victor ...(?)... So he went to Columbia, this man understood, and let him make a record. They did "The Crazy Blues," and it swept the country, and that's when they started looking for Blues singers like crazy. There was Mamie Smith, then there was Bessie Smith, there was Clara Smith, there was Trixie Smith, there was Sara Smith, Emma Smith, Beulah Smith, Saponia Smith -- as long as you had a Smith. And that big old Smith name in…

Well, how many Smiths have you got in the Baptist Church? It would be two million of 'em. So you'd get all the chicks could sing, I could understand why Whites sometimes were leery about how many Blacks they let through.
